domains.name: Claude Models, Prompting, and Context Engineering

questions.stem: A support team wants answers to product questions grounded in a 300-page manual. Questions are single-turn, and the manual is updated monthly. What is the simplest sufficient architecture?

options.a: Retrieval over the manual feeding one model call that cites the passages it used
options.b: A multi-agent research system with a planner and three specialist agents for the manual
options.c: An autonomous agent that browses the manual page by page until it finds the answer
options.d: A model fine-tuned on the manual every month, so the answers always reflect the latest version

questions.explanation: One well-scoped, grounded call meets the requirement, so retrieval plus a single call is the simplest sufficient pattern ({a}). {b} and {c} add autonomy the task doesn't need, with the cost and latency to match. Monthly fine-tuning ({d}) is heavy, slower to update than re-indexing, and gives no citations.

questions.stem: Which architecture proposal for an invoice-processing assistant is complete?

options.a: Intake and OCR; extraction with schema validation; ERP posting with an exceptions queue; evals and corrections fed back
options.b: Email intake and OCR; extraction with the most capable model at high effort; posting straight into the ERP system
options.c: Extraction with schema validation; posting to the ERP with an exceptions queue; a dashboard of monthly invoice volume
options.d: Email intake and OCR; a multi-agent extraction team with a reviewer agent; posting to the ERP; a launch announcement

questions.explanation: A complete architecture has input, processing, output and a feedback loop that turns evals, user corrections and monitoring into design changes ({a}). {b} has no feedback loop. {c} has no input stage, and a volume dashboard measures activity without feeding quality back. {d} adds complexity and still has no feedback loop.

questions.stem: Two designs meet the accuracy target. Design 1 uses the top tier: p95 latency 6 seconds, $0.09 per request. Design 2 routes between the fast and balanced tiers: p95 latency 2 seconds, $0.02 per request. The client's stated constraint is a 3-second p95 SLA at 2 million requests a month. Which design, and why?

options.a: Design 2, because it meets the latency SLA and the cost pillar at the same accuracy
options.b: Design 1, because the top tier leaves quality headroom for harder requests later on
options.c: Run both designs in production indefinitely and let the traffic decide over time
options.d: Postpone the decision until a newer model is released, since prices keep falling

questions.explanation: When both options meet accuracy, the stated business constraint decides, and only Design 2 meets the 3-second SLA, at about $40,000 a month against $180,000 ({a}). {b} breaks the SLA. {c} doubles cost and complexity for no reason. {d} ignores a decision the data already supports.

questions.stem: A due-diligence system must analyze each target company's financials, legal filings and press coverage. The three analyses are independent, and each needs different tools and sources. Which design fits?

options.a: An orchestrator with three scoped subagents running in parallel, then a synthesis step
options.b: One agent holding all the tools for all three analyses, so a single context sees everything
options.c: One agent doing the three analyses in sequence, finishing each before it starts the next
options.d: Three separate systems, one per analysis, each delivering its own report to the client

questions.explanation: Independent subtasks with different tool needs are what justifies decomposition: each subagent gets a narrow toolset and its own context, and the orchestrator merges the results ({a}). {b} is capability bloat. {c} gives up parallelism and mixes three contexts. {d} skips the synthesis the client actually needs.

questions.stem: A global retailer's policy assistant covers 14 regions. Each region's policies differ and are owned by different teams. Answers mix rules from different regions. What is the best design change?

options.a: Tag documents with their region and filter retrieval by the user's region before semantic search
options.b: Fourteen regional agents that negotiate with each other on every question until they agree
options.c: Put all 14 regions' policies in every request, so that the model always has the complete set to work from
options.d: Ask users to mention their region in each question, and change nothing else in the system

questions.explanation: The data has a clean partition, so filtering on region metadata keeps other regions' rules out of the context ({a}). {b} adds coordination machinery to a retrieval problem. {c} is context stuffing. {d} leaves the mixed retrieval in place.

questions.stem: Which TWO workloads benefit most from prompt caching? (Select TWO)

options.a: An agent loop that resends the same 12,000-token system prompt and tool definitions on every turn
options.b: An endpoint where many users ask questions about the same 50-page policy within minutes of each other
options.c: A weekly job that sends one unique 3,000-token prompt, different every time it runs
options.d: Requests whose first line is the current timestamp, followed by a long, stable policy text that never changes
options.e: Single requests shorter than the minimum cacheable length, sent thousands of times a day

questions.explanation: Caching pays off when a long, stable prefix repeats within the cache lifetime ({a}, {b}). A weekly unique prompt ({c}) never repeats in time. A timestamp at the start ({d}) breaks the prefix on every request. Prompts under the minimum length ({e}) are never cached.

questions.stem: An eligibility step must apply six interacting rules. Accuracy is the priority, and the latency budget is generous. Which prompting approach fits?

options.a: Have the model reason through each rule, stated as an explicit criterion, before deciding, then validate the result
options.b: A zero-shot prompt kept as short as possible, so that the model isn't distracted by the detail of the six rules
options.c: Few-shot examples alone, with no stated rules, so the model infers the logic from the cases
options.d: A lower effort level, so that the model commits to an answer before it overthinks the interacting rules

questions.explanation: Multi-step logic benefits from explicit reasoning before the answer, and the generous latency budget covers its cost ({a}). Zero-shot ({b}) suits simple, unambiguous tasks. Examples ({c}) teach format and edge cases, and six interacting rules still need to be stated. Lower effort ({d}) cuts the reasoning the task needs.

questions.stem: An enterprise assistant's system prompt has grown to 60,000 tokens of procedures for 40 business processes, and most requests need one or two of them. Latency and cost are high, and instruction-following has slipped. What is the best restructuring?

options.a: Keep the system prompt to the core role and rules, and load each procedure as a Skill only when relevant
options.b: Mark the most important procedures in capitals so the model gives them priority over the rest
options.c: Move to a model with a larger context window, so that all 40 procedures fit with plenty of room to spare
options.d: Build 40 separate assistants, one per business process, and make users choose the right one

questions.explanation: Loading procedures on demand keeps the context small and focused, which improves attention, cost and latency together ({a}). Emphasis ({b}) doesn't shrink the prompt. A bigger window ({c}) holds more of the same dilution. {d} moves the routing problem onto users.

questions.stem: Downstream systems consume the assistant's JSON, and occasional schema violations cause failed transactions. Which change addresses this at the source, and what still needs checking?

options.a: Structured outputs with the integration schema, plus semantic checks and handling of refusal and length stops
options.b: A retry loop that resends any request whose JSON fails validation, until a valid response arrives
options.c: A stronger instruction to follow the schema exactly, repeated at the end of the system prompt
options.d: A regex step that repairs broken JSON before it is passed on to the downstream systems

questions.explanation: Constrained decoding removes schema violations at the source, and semantic checks plus stop-reason handling cover what it doesn't guarantee ({a}). Retries ({b}) and instructions ({c}) reduce failures without eliminating them. Regex repair ({d}) guesses at intent and can corrupt data quietly.

questions.stem: A procurement agent must get quotes from a supplier's own AI agent, which runs on the supplier's systems with its own tools, policies and reasoning. Which integration mechanism fits?

options.a: Agent-to-agent delegation over a defined protocol, with request and response contracts and auth
options.b: An MCP server that gives your agent direct access to the supplier's database of current prices
options.c: A direct API call to Claude with the supplier's price list pasted into the prompt for each quote
options.d: A shared system prompt that both companies edit, so the two agents follow the same instructions

questions.explanation: Two autonomous systems with separate owners, tools and policies call for delegation between agents, with contracts and isolation so either side can fail independently ({a}). {b} bypasses the supplier's agent and policies and assumes access you won't get. {c} works only if you already have current prices, which is what you're asking for. {d} merges two organizations' control into one prompt.

questions.stem: One internal app sends support tickets to Claude for tagging. One team owns it, and no reuse is planned. A platform engineer proposes building an MCP server first. What is the right assessment?

options.a: Use a direct API integration now, and revisit MCP if other surfaces later need the capability
options.b: Build the MCP server now, since every integration should go through MCP as a matter of standard
options.c: Use agent-to-agent delegation between the ticketing app and a dedicated tagging agent
options.d: Fine-tune a tagging model instead, so the app no longer needs to call Claude at all

questions.explanation: MCP pays off when one capability serves many clients or surfaces, and one app with one owner is the direct-API case ({a}). {b} adds maintenance for a benefit that doesn't exist yet. {c} adds autonomous-system machinery to a single call. {d} skips a simpler option that works.

questions.stem: Which TWO observations are signs of capability bloat in a production agent? (Select TWO)

options.a: It exposes 45 tools, and invocation logs show only 9 ever used
options.b: Two tools have overlapping descriptions, and both plausibly handle 'find a customer'
options.c: Each subagent's tools are scoped to the single responsibility it has in the system
options.d: The reporting agent uses read-only credentials for the databases it queries
options.e: Tool descriptions state when not to use each tool

questions.explanation: Unused tools that ship with every request ({a}) and overlapping tools that blur selection ({b}) are classic signs of bloat. Scoped toolsets ({c}), read-only credentials for a read-only job ({d}) and boundary statements in descriptions ({e}) are the cure.

questions.stem: An agent connects to six MCP servers exposing 300 tools, and every request front-loads all of their definitions. Tool selection is poor and costs are high. What is the best fix?

options.a: Load tool definitions on demand, such as with tool search, and give each agent only the servers it needs
options.b: Move to a model with a larger context window, so that all 300 definitions fit comfortably
options.c: Shorten every tool description to a single line, so the definitions take up fewer tokens
options.d: Add more examples to the system prompt showing which tool to pick for each of the common kinds of request

questions.explanation: Loading tools as the agent narrows in cuts tokens and improves selection accuracy, and scoping servers per responsibility removes tools that never belonged ({a}). A bigger window ({b}) holds the same noise. One-line descriptions ({c}) make selection worse. Examples ({d}) add tokens without reducing the tool count.

questions.stem: A company assistant answers questions over the document store using a service account that can read every folder, including HR and legal. A contractor asked about salaries and got an answer. What is the root fix?

options.a: Run retrieval and tools with the calling user's identity and permissions, and log each access
options.b: Add a system-prompt rule, 'Never discuss salaries', and repeat it at the start of each turn
options.c: Remove the HR documents from the index, so that the assistant can no longer retrieve them
options.d: Filter out any response that contains the word 'salary' before it reaches the contractor's screen

questions.explanation: The shared over-privileged account erased per-user authorization and made every access unattributable, so the fix is acting as the caller ({a}). {b} is a probabilistic patch, {c} breaks legitimate HR use, and {d} is easy to get around and blocks legitimate answers.

questions.stem: Engineers search an internal knowledge base with exact error codes such as 'E-4031.' Semantic search returns conceptually similar documents about other errors. What is the best fix?

options.a: Hybrid search: keyword matching for exact identifiers plus semantic search, then re-ranking
options.b: A larger embedding model, which captures the meaning of each individual error code more precisely
options.c: Retrieve more chunks per query, so that the right document is more likely to be included
options.d: Fine-tune the generation model on the error codes, so that it recognizes each one on sight

questions.explanation: Exact identifiers such as error codes and SKUs need keyword matching, which hybrid search adds alongside semantic retrieval ({a}). Better embeddings ({b}) still treat codes as fuzzy meaning. More chunks ({c}) add noise. The generation model ({d}) can't fix documents that were never retrieved.

questions.stem: A contract-extraction service has three complaints: wrong values, slow responses at peak hours, and a rising monthly bill. Which THREE metrics should the monitoring plan track? (Select THREE)

options.a: Field-level accuracy against a labeled dataset
options.b: p95 and p99 latency
options.c: Cost per document and tokens per task
options.d: Number of prompt revisions per month

questions.explanation: Each complaint maps to a metric: wrong values to accuracy ({a}), slowness to tail latency ({b}), and the bill to cost per unit of work ({c}). Prompt revision counts ({d}) and response length ({e}) measure activity, and neither shows whether the complaints are fixed.

questions.stem: A team tuned its prompt against the same 200 examples it uses to report accuracy. Testing shows 98%, and production shows 84%. What went wrong, and what is the fix?

options.a: The eval set leaked into tuning; tune on a development set and report on a held-out set like production
options.b: Production traffic is lower quality than the test examples, so it should be filtered before the model sees it
options.c: The model is too small for the variety in production, so the system should move up a tier
options.d: 200 examples is too few to be reliable, so the team should add 20 more of the same kind

questions.explanation: Tuning against the test set overfits to it, so the score stops predicting production ({a}). {b} blames the data the system has to handle. {c} changes the model without fixing the measurement. {d} keeps the same leak with a slightly bigger set.

questions.stem: A team wants to ship a new prompt, new retrieval settings and a tier change together, because 'it felt better in 15 spot checks.' What is the correct approach?

options.a: Test one variable at a time, with a metric and sample size set in advance, and ship on a significant result
options.b: Ship all three changes together, since the spot checks were positive and it saves a release
options.c: Ask the stakeholders which version they prefer after a short demo of both versions
options.d: Run 15 more spot checks with a different reviewer to confirm the first impression

questions.explanation: A clean experiment changes one variable and decides on a metric chosen in advance ({a}). With three changes at once ({b}), a win or a loss can't be attributed to anything. Preference ({c}) and more spot checks ({d}) are still the feels-better method.

questions.stem: Traces show the correct policy passages are retrieved, yet answers still state the wrong refund window. Where is the failure, and what is the first fix?

options.a: Generation: answer only from the retrieved passages, cite them, and evaluate faithfulness
options.b: Retrieval: re-chunk and re-embed the whole corpus, so the passages match questions more closely
options.c: The index is stale, so it should be rebuilt from the latest version of every policy document
options.d: Too few passages: raise the number retrieved per question so the model has more to go on

questions.explanation: When the right documents arrive and the answer is still wrong, the failure sits in generation and grounding ({a}). {b} and {c} fix retrieval, which the traces show is working. {d} adds noise to a context that already contains the answer.

questions.stem: Answers about leave policies leave out exceptions. Traces show the retrieved chunks contain the rule sentence, while the exception sits in the next paragraph, which isn't retrieved. What is the best fix?

options.a: Re-chunk along the document's structure, with some overlap, so rules and exceptions stay together
options.b: Retrieve 30 chunks instead of 5, so the paragraph with the exception is more likely to be included
options.c: Move to a more capable model, which is better at inferring exceptions from the rule sentence
options.d: Tell the model in the system prompt to remember that most policies have exceptions

questions.explanation: Chunks smaller than the unit of meaning split rules from their qualifiers, so structure-aware chunking fixes the retrieval unit ({a}). More chunks ({b}) might catch the exception along with plenty of noise. No model ({c}) can use a paragraph it never receives, and an instruction ({d}) can't supply the missing text.

questions.stem: An agent reads inbound customer emails and can issue refunds. Which TWO controls are deterministic, as opposed to prompt-based? (Select TWO)

options.a: Tool permissions that cap a refund at $100 per call and send larger amounts for human approval
options.b: An output filter that blocks any reply containing a full account number
options.c: A system-prompt rule, 'Never issue large refunds', placed at the top of the agent's instructions
options.d: A persona instruction, 'You are a careful agent', repeated before each tool call
options.e: Few-shot examples of the agent declining suspicious requests

questions.explanation: Permission limits ({a}) and output filtering ({b}) are enforced in code, whatever the model decides. {c}, {d} and {e} shape behavior probabilistically, and a cleverly written email can talk the model past them.

questions.stem: A moderation pipeline handles 500,000 low-risk comments a day and occasionally receives legal threats. Which human-in-the-loop design fits?

options.a: Automate routine decisions with sampled QA; send legal threats and low-score cases to reviewers
options.b: Have a human review every comment before it is published, so nothing slips through
options.c: Remove humans from the pipeline entirely, since the comments are low risk on the whole
options.d: Let the model escalate to a human whenever its self-reported confidence is low

questions.explanation: Humans go where the risk is high, and sampling covers the routine volume ({a}). Reviewing everything ({b}) destroys the efficiency case. {c} leaves legal threats unhandled. Self-reported confidence ({d}) is poorly calibrated, so the thresholds that route cases to people have to be set by the system.

questions.stem: A US telehealth company with patients in the US and Germany plans to use Claude to summarize clinical notes. Which TWO frameworks apply? (Select TWO)

options.a: HIPAA, for US patients' health information
options.b: GDPR, for the personal data of patients in the EU
options.c: FedRAMP
options.d: Only HIPAA, since the company is based in the US
options.e: None, since Claude is a third-party service

questions.explanation: The framework follows the data type and the jurisdiction: US health data brings HIPAA ({a}), and processing EU residents' personal data brings GDPR wherever the company is based ({b}). FedRAMP ({c}) covers cloud services for US federal agencies. {d} ignores the German patients, and {e} confuses using a vendor with being exempt.

questions.stem: Your observability stack stores full prompts and responses, including customer personal data, in a log platform that 300 engineers can read. What is the risk, and what is the fix?

options.a: Data leakage through logs: redact personal data first, restrict access, and set a retention limit
options.b: No real risk, because the logs are internal and every one of the 300 engineers works for the company
options.c: Encrypt the stored logs at rest and leave the access as it is for the 300 engineers
options.d: Ask the model in the system prompt to leave personal data out of every one of its responses

questions.explanation: Logs and traces are a leakage channel, so the fix minimizes what's stored and who can see it ({a}). Internal access ({b}) still exposes customer data to hundreds of people. Encryption with unchanged access ({c}) protects the storage while every reader still sees the data. {d} leaves the personal data in the prompts, and the model can't be relied on to keep it out of responses.

questions.stem: A resume-screening assistant ranks candidates for interviews. An audit finds that applicants from two universities abroad are ranked lower than equally qualified applicants. The candidate pool is balanced, and the system prompt tells the model to favor 'polished communication and familiarity with US business norms.' What is the source of the bias, and the right mitigation?

options.a: Prompt framing: use job-related criteria applied identically to everyone, then re-measure by group
options.b: Data bias: collect more resumes from the two universities so the model sees more of their graduates
options.c: Evaluation design: change the audit's test set until the gap between the groups disappears
options.d: Model choice: move to a more capable tier, which judges candidates from abroad more fairly

questions.explanation: The pool is balanced and the prompt itself encodes criteria that disadvantage the group, so the bias comes from prompt framing and the fix is neutral, job-related criteria, checked per group ({a}). More data ({b}) treats a data problem the audit didn't find. Changing the test set ({c}) hides the gap without fixing it. A stronger model ({d}) follows the same loaded instructions.

questions.stem: Stakeholders ask for a guarantee that the assistant 'never gives a wrong answer.' What is the appropriate response?

options.a: Commit to measured targets: accuracy per slice, an error budget, escalation paths, and a remediation plan
options.b: Promise 100% accuracy to secure approval, then work toward it during the first months in production
options.c: Refuse to set any accuracy target, since no LLM system can promise a specific level of quality
options.d: Commit only to 99.9% uptime, which the platform can guarantee, and leave accuracy out of the SLA

questions.explanation: Probabilistic systems get SLAs built on measured rates, such as at least 96% accuracy per slice on a held-out set, with error budgets, escalation paths and remediation, and stakeholders should hear that LLM outputs have a measurable error rate ({a}). {b} sets up a broken promise. {c} leaves stakeholders nothing to hold the system to. Uptime ({d}) says nothing about answer quality.

questions.stem: Which TWO artifacts belong in the handoff to the team that will operate the system? (Select TWO)

options.a: Runbooks covering escalation paths and known failure modes
options.b: Eval baselines and an inventory of prompts and their versions
options.c: The architect's personal working notes from the design phase
options.d: The kickoff slide deck that set out the project's goals and scope
options.e: A raw export of the project chat channel from start to finish

questions.explanation: Operators need to know how to respond to problems ({a}) and what normal looks like, along with what is deployed ({b}). Personal notes ({c}), kickoff slides ({d}) and raw chat ({e}) aren't operational documentation.

questions.stem: Claude Code runs in your CI pipeline, and the team agrees it must never run git push or curl anywhere the repository is used. Where should this restriction live?

options.a: Deny rules in the committed project settings, such as `Bash(git push *)` and `Bash(curl *)`
options.b: Each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json`, set up during onboarding for the team
options.c: A `CLAUDE.md` instruction at the top of the repository saying never to run git push or call curl
options.d: A wiki page listing the commands that Claude Code must never run in any pipeline

questions.explanation: Permission rules in version-controlled project settings apply everywhere the repository runs, CI included, and the client enforces them ({a}). User settings ({b}) don't reach CI or other developers. `CLAUDE.md` ({c}) is guidance the model weighs. A wiki ({d}) is invisible to the tooling.

questions.stem: A platform team built a code-review subagent and a release-notes skill that every repository in the company should use, in the same version. What is the best way to distribute them?

options.a: Package them as a plugin, or deploy them through managed settings, so everyone gets one version
options.b: Post the prompt text in a chat channel for developers to copy into their own setups
options.c: Ask each developer to copy the files into their own `~/.claude/` folder during onboarding
options.d: Paste both definitions into every repository's `CLAUDE.md`, so each project carries them

questions.explanation: Plugins bundle skills and subagents for distribution, and managed settings can push them to the whole organization, which keeps one maintained version ({a}). Copy-and-paste distribution ({b}, {c}) drifts as soon as the originals change. `CLAUDE.md` ({d}) holds always-on instructions and can't define a subagent or an on-demand skill.

questions.stem: A team adopting Claude Code configured its repository so that pull requests written by Claude merge automatically once CI passes. A production incident traces back to one of those merges, and nobody on the team can explain the change. Which control restores human ownership of the code?

options.a: Require a named human reviewer to approve every pull request, AI-written ones included
options.b: Have a second Claude session review each pull request before it merges into the main branch
options.c: Raise the test coverage threshold for AI-written pull requests before they can merge
options.d: Label AI-written pull requests so that they are easy to find after any later incident

questions.explanation: Ownership means a person approves and answers for each change before it merges ({a}). An AI reviewer ({b}) adds a check without adding accountability. More coverage ({c}) catches more defects but still leaves nobody owning the change. A label ({d}) helps after an incident and does nothing before one.
